title: Why do we suffer?
hookLine: every tradition asks it, and each answers differently

cards: A man blind from birth is sitting by the road. A teacher and his students walk past, and the students ask out loud, right there: whose fault is this? Did this man do something wrong, or did his parents?
It's an old question, and a hard one to hear about yourself. When something terrible happens, the nearest reason to hand is often blame. Today, the year's first great question: why do we suffer?
Four answers, each in its own voice.

teach.b: First, the Gospel of John. The disciples ask, "Master, who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind?"
And Jesus answers, "Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him." Then he heals him.
There's a lot in the rest of that answer, but its first word is plain: neither. The shortcut to blame is closed. Second, the Qur'an.
In the second surah, God says that people will be tried with something of fear and hunger, and loss of wealth and lives and crops, and then: give glad tidings to the steadfast.
Hardship, in this answer, is a test, and the response it asks for is steadfastness. The Arabic word behind it is sabr, patience that holds.

Third, the Buddha. In his first teaching he names suffering, then where it comes from: a craving, a thirst, always reaching for more and for something else. We'll spend the coming days inside that answer.
Fourth, the Stoic Epictetus. His Handbook says that what troubles people isn't the things that happen, but their judgments about them.
Death isn't terrible, or Socrates would have thought so; the terror is in our opinion of death. A test met with patience. A thirst.
A judgment. And a story where blame is refused, and the story moves on to healing. They don't line up into one tidy reply, and this year won't force them to.

how: Some people bring suffering to their own tradition's texts and teachers: Christians to the Gospels and prayer, Muslims to the Qur'an and the practice of patience, Buddhists to the four noble truths, students of Stoicism to the Handbook.

o: a fast kept through a hard season
a quiet sadness accepted without a word
patience that holds steady under trial

p: neither this man sinned, nor his parents
a test, met by the steadfast

the Qur'an gives glad tidings to the steadfast

Epictetus says death is terrible, as Socrates taught
he says if death were terrible, Socrates would have thought so; the terror is in the opinion.

games.q: you're walking with the disciples past a man blind from birth. someone asks whose fault it is. what's the answer in the story?
o: neither he nor his parents sinned
games.why: John 9:3: "Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents." then Jesus heals him.

practice: Let one real weight you carry come to mind, an ache, a worry, a loss; it needn't be the heaviest, and it needn't have words yet.

Then let the four answers pass by it like visitors at a bedside: a test, a thirst, a judgment, neither he nor his parents. You don't have to agree with any of them; just notice which visitor you'd let stay a little longer.

wordCard.voice: Sabr, the Arabic word for patience that holds steady under trial, the response the Qur'an asks of the steadfast. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: patience that holds steady under trial; the Qur'an's word for the steadfast in 2:155 comes from it.

carryVoice: Your line: each answers differently. One question, four voices, no blending. Day six hundred ninety-nine.
